name: Language of the Birds
teaser: Books take flight above a busy corner.
story: Look up at the books suspended above Columbus and Broadway: their open pages take the poses of birds in flight. Brian Goggin and Dorka Keehn designed this 2008 installation for the pedestrian plaza linking Chinatown and North Beach.
facts: Goggin, Brian and Keehn, Dorka · 2008 · Nw Corner
sourceName: SF Arts Commission · Civic Art Collection

name: Plaything of the Wind
teaser: A wall with a second life for broken dishes.
story: Look closely at the wall outside the Betty Ann Ong recreation center. Colette Crutcher’s 2012 work brings ceramic tile, crockery, glass and recycled mirrors together. Try picking out a familiar material inside the larger composition.
facts: Crutcher, Colette · 2012 · Ceramic tile, crockery, glass, recycled mirrors, grout and cement board · Playground Exterior South Wall
sourceName: SF Arts Commission · Civic Art Collection

name: Bronze Icosaspirale
teaser: A bronze puzzle worth walking around.
story: Charles O. Perry’s 1966 bronze stands near Davis and Washington. Circle it and compare the spaces you can see through from each side. A change of viewpoint is part of the pleasure of finding sculpture on an ordinary walk.
facts: Perry, Charles O. · 1966 · Bronze · Northwest Corner; Park is boarded by Clay St, Washinton St., Davis St., and Drumm St.
sourceName: SF Arts Commission · Civic Art Collection

name: Mechanics Monument
teaser: A monument to the people who made things.
story: Douglas Tilden’s bronze monument has stood at Market and Bush since 1901. Dedicated to Peter Donahue and given to the city by James Mervyn Donahue, it puts the word “mechanics” into the middle of the Financial District. Pause to study the figures before joining the foot traffic again.
facts: Tilden, Douglas · 1901 · Bronze · NE Corner, Mechanics Monument Plaza
sourceName: SF Arts Commission · Civic Art Collection

name: Bay Bench
teaser: Your waterfront rest stop is also an artwork.
story: Before heading onto Pier 7, notice the bench at its entrance. Steve Gillman’s Bay Bench pairs sunset-red granite with bronze. It was commissioned for the pier in 1990: a reminder that public art can be something you sit beside, rather than something you hurry past.
facts: Gillman, Steve · 1990 · Sunset red granite, bronze · Flanking Entrance
sourceName: SF Arts Commission · Civic Art Collection

name: Passage
teaser: A sculpture hiding at the edge of the game.
story: Look along the playing fields at Moscone Recreation Center for Kent Roberts’s Passage. The 2010 work uses stainless steel and concrete. Its everyday sports-park setting is an invitation to look for art outside the usual gallery places.
facts: Roberts, Kent · 2010 · Stainless steel and concrete · Edge Of Playing Fields; park boarded by Laguna, Bay, Chestnut and Webster Streets
sourceName: SF Arts Commission · Civic Art Collection

name: ILWU Memorial
teaser: Waterfront labor, remembered in painted steel.
story: At Mission and Steuart, look for the International Longshoremen’s and Warehousemen’s Union memorial. The artists’ collective M.E.T.A.L.—Mural Environmentalists Together in Art Labor—made the painted-steel work in 1986. Even the artists’ name ties art to work.
facts: M.E.T.A.L. (Mural Environmentalists Together in Art Labor) · 1986 · Painted steel · SW corner of Hotel Vitale
sourceName: SF Arts Commission · Civic Art Collection

name: Boeddeker’s Blooming Bounty
teaser: Steel gets a botanical title.
story: At the Eddy and Jones corner of Boeddeker Park, find Amy Blackstone’s Boeddeker’s Blooming Bounty. The city dates this steel work to 2014. Compare that exuberant title with the shapes you can pick out at the park’s edge.
facts: Blackstone, Amy · 2014 · Steel · Corner Of Jones
sourceName: SF Arts Commission · Civic Art Collection

name: Sea Change
teaser: A steel encounter beside the waterfront.
story: Find Mark di Suvero’s Sea Change by Second and King. This 1995 work combines painted and stainless steel. Step back, then look again from another angle: the waterfront gives a sculpture a very different backdrop from a museum wall.
facts: di Suvero, Mark · 1995 · Painted and stainless steel · Waterfront Park
sourceName: SF Arts Commission · Civic Art Collection

name: Auspicious Clouds / Heavy Fog
teaser: San Francisco weather, translated into steel.
story: Michael Arcega’s painted-steel work on Broadway is part of Auspicious Clouds / Heavy Fog. This piece carries the color name “Silver Blue.” Look for it near Powell, and compare its color with whatever the sky is doing today.
facts: Arcega, Michael · Painted Steel · Chinatown; Broadway Street between the east end of the Robert C. Levy Tunnel and Columbus Avenue; on sidewalk near intersection of Broadway and Powell Streets
sourceName: SF Arts Commission · Civic Art Collection

name: Origami Fountains
teaser: Paper-folding meets bronze.
story: Ruth Asawa’s Origami Fountains sit on the Buchanan pedestrian walkway between Post and Sutter. The city records the pair as bronze works from 1999. Look for the connection between the title’s folded paper and the much more permanent material.
facts: Asawa, Ruth · 1999 · Bronze · In middle of Buchannan pedestrian walkway; Between Post And Sutter St.
sourceName: SF Arts Commission · Civic Art Collection

name: Fountain of the Tortoises
teaser: A small creature hunt on Nob Hill.
story: In the middle of Huntington Park, look for the Fountain of the Tortoises. The city’s collection record lists marble and bronze. Let the name turn a quick glance into a closer inspection: how many tortoises can you find?
facts: Taddeo · 1900 · Marble and bronze · In center of park, Park boarded by Taylor, Sacramento, California and Cushman Streets
sourceName: SF Arts Commission · Civic Art Collection

name: Skygate
teaser: The sky has a frame.
story: Roger Barr’s Skygate stands on the waterfront between Piers 35 and 39. Made in 1985 from mirror-finished stainless steel, it offers a reason to watch how an artwork changes with light and surroundings.
facts: Barr, Roger · 1985 · Mirror finished stainless steel Type 316 L · In the Public Park on the water side of Embarcadero, Between Piers 35 And 39
sourceName: SF Arts Commission · Civic Art Collection

name: Sun Yat-Sen
teaser: A portrait in steel and rose-red stone.
story: Find Beniamino Bufano’s Sun Yat-Sen near the Quincy Street side of St. Mary’s Square. The 1936 work combines stainless steel with rose-red granite. Look at how those two materials divide the figure.
facts: Bufano, Beniamino · 1936 · Stainless steel, rose-red granite · Square is boarded by Quincy Street Between California Street and Pine Streets; statue is closer to the the middle of the Quincy Street side
sourceName: SF Arts Commission · Civic Art Collection

name: Playland Revisited
teaser: A beachside detour into an artwork’s memories.
story: At Cabrillo and La Playa, find Ray Beldner’s Playland Revisited. The city lists stainless-steel mesh over a steel framework, with photo-etched plaques. Give the plaques a closer look; they are part of the work, not just its label.
facts: Beldner, Ray · 1996 · Stainless steel mesh over steel armature with photo-etched plaques · Northeast Intersection Corner
sourceName: SF Arts Commission · Civic Art Collection

name: Incomplete Metamorphosis (Dragonfly)
teaser: An insect rendered in aluminum.
story: Look for Joyce Hsu’s dragonfly at the 19th Avenue entrance between Geary and Anza. The aluminum work is part of Incomplete Metamorphosis. Its title makes this a good place to notice how artists borrow shapes from living things.
facts: Hsu, Joyce · 2006 · Aluminum · 19Th Ave. Entrance Between Geary Blvd. And Anza St.
sourceName: SF Arts Commission · Civic Art Collection

name: Ina Coolbrith Park
teaser: A small climb with a much bigger view.
story: This little hillside park makes you earn its city-and-bay views. Take the climb slowly, then pause before heading back into the streets. San Francisco Recreation and Parks describes it as a small pocket of Russian Hill, despite the property dataset’s broader Nob Hill neighborhood label.
facts: Ina Coolbrith Park. Neighborhood Park or Playground. 0.87 acres in the city property record.
sourceName: SF Recreation & Parks

name: Francisco Park
teaser: A reservoir’s second life.
story: This hillside held an unused, fenced-off reservoir for decades before becoming Francisco Park in April 2022. Today its terraces look toward the bay, and a rainwater-catchment system helps water the landscape. The city’s old water infrastructure has become a place to linger.
facts: Francisco Park. Neighborhood Park or Playground. 4.89 acres in the city property record.
sourceName: SF Recreation & Parks

name: Fay Park
teaser: Twin gazebos, tucked into the hillside.
story: Three garden terraces climb half a block at Fay Park, linked by stairs and ramps. Look for the two latticed wooden gazebos at the top, above boxwood hedges and stone walls. It is a small place that rewards slowing down.
facts: Fay Park. Mini Park. 0.33 acres in the city property record.
sourceName: SF Recreation & Parks

name: Lafayette Park
teaser: A public park with a private holdout.
story: Securing Lafayette Park as public space took decades of competing claims. The city finally settled that struggle in 1936—with the St. Regis Apartments remaining a private exception. A walk here is also a chance to think about who gets to claim a piece of the city.
facts: Lafayette Park. Neighborhood Park or Playground. 12.48 acres in the city property record.
sourceName: SF Recreation & Parks

name: Alta Plaza Park
teaser: A former quarry with a new outlook.
story: This hilltop park occupies four blocks of Pacific Heights. City project records identify it as a former quarry; today the high ground offers views north toward the bay and south across the city. Look beyond the lawns and imagine the land before it became a park.
facts: Alta Plaza Park. Neighborhood Park or Playground. 12.94 acres in the city property record.
sourceName: SF Recreation & Parks

name: South Park
teaser: A strolling park, reinvented.
story: South Park began with the idea of an English picturesque strolling park. Its 2017 renovation added paths, a meadow, play space and places to sit. Take a slow circuit and notice how much fits into this pocket of South of Market.
facts: South Park. Neighborhood Park or Playground. 1.12 acres in the city property record.
sourceName: SF Recreation & Parks

name: Allyne Park
teaser: Room for a pause, without a big detour.
story: At 2609 Gough Street, Allyne Park offers a small lawn rather than a full sports complex. The city lists it as less than an acre. This is a stop for sitting and looking around, not for adding another long item to your itinerary.
facts: Allyne Park. Neighborhood Park or Playground. 0.88 acres in the city property record.
sourceName: SF Recreation & Parks

name: Cottage Row Mini Park
teaser: A little garden with a name to investigate.
story: Cottage Row’s mini park includes the Issei Garden. A 2019 Recreation and Park Commission agenda documents a proposal for a plaque on a boulder there. Look for the garden and its interpretation as you pass through this small patch of Pacific Heights.
facts: Cottage Row Mini Park. Mini Park. 0.17 acres in the city property record.
sourceName: SF Recreation & Parks
